title: Felix and the Wreath Thief
markdown:
It was the eve of the school’s grand sports day, a day usually buzzing with excitement and the buttery smell of popcorn.

Felix the ferret was a whirlwind of fur and fizz, usually darting like a dropped marble, nose twitching with a thousand questions. This morning he was in a terrible worry. The champion’s prize — a magnificent laurel wreath, deep green leaves that smelled of sunshine and victory — had vanished. It had sat proudly on its velvet cushion. Now only an empty space. A strange shivery feeling rippled from his twitching nose to his perky tail. A wobbly, tummy-tumbling feeling, not at all like Felix.

He scurried around the prize table, legs a blur. He nudged a forgotten ribbon. He sniffed a juice box. Nothing.

Then a soft rustle, like turning pages or silk on a breeze. Dot, the library ghost, see-through and calm as morning mist, a smile that shimmered like moonlight. A friend to all, a quiet keeper of stories and lost socks, very good at finding things that had wandered. “Felix, my dear. What’s troubling your whiskers?”

Felix’s voice was a frantic squeak. “The wreath. The champion’s wreath. Gone. Sports day starts soon. What will happen?”

Dot floated closer. “Let us investigate. The library often holds answers. Every lost thing has a story.” A curious ferret and a graceful ghost set off.

First the busy schoolyard: bright colours, happy shouts, banners dancing. They asked a grumpy crow who claimed he had seen only crumbs. They consulted a wise-looking garden gnome who, after a long blink, offered no help. The sun climbed. Cheers for the first races began. Without the wreath the prize ceremony would be rather disappointing.

Dot, with her keen nose for anything old, caught a faint earthy scent. Not popcorn. Not grass. Older, drier, something olive-y. “This way.”

They followed it away from the cheering crowds toward the ancient olive grove beside the school. A quiet sleepy place, gnarled trees whispering old secrets, branches like wise old arms. And there, in the library’s dusty archives — Dot had looped them through a side door first — a brittle yellowed scroll, smelling of old paper.

Dot guided Felix’s nose. “Look. It tells of the very first Olympics. No medals then. Winners were crowned with wreaths of olive leaves.”

Felix’s fur tingled. He imagined ancient athletes, strong and proud. The scroll fluttered. A cheeky breeze scattered dry leaves. For a moment the clue seemed hidden. Felix’s heart lurched.

His nose, now tuned to that ancient olive scent, did not falter. “Stronger here.” He nudged Dot toward a particularly old moss-covered olive tree, roots like a tangled beard. Nestled among them, munching happily on what looked like fallen leaves, was the largest, slowest tortoise Felix had ever seen. Shell like a tiny mountain. Peeking from beneath it, a little nibbled but intact: the missing laurel wreath.

“He thought it was a salad.” A giggle escaped. The tortoise blinked, unperturbed, and let out a slow contented sigh, very pleased with its leafy snack.

With Dot’s gentle guidance Felix retrieved the wreath. A bit wobbly, a few missing leaves, but there. They raced back, fuzzy brown fur and shimmering phantom silk, arriving as the last event — the three-legged race — finished.

Felix, panting, tail high, presented the slightly chewed laurel wreath. A cheer washed the schoolyard. The champion, Lily, brilliant at the long jump, accepted it with a beaming smile and, with a wink at Felix, placed it carefully on her head.

As the sun dipped, long golden shadows, Felix and Dot sat under the old oak. The worry had gone, replaced by the warm glow of a shared adventure. Lily’s wreath sat a little crooked and a little nibbled, which somehow made it look more like a prize. Dot smiled her moonlight smile. Felix’s nose, for once, had no more questions — only the faint, happy smell of olive and popcorn.
